title: Lucas' Theorem
directAnswer: The factorial-inverse method for nCr mod p assumes p > n. When n can be far larger than p (and p is small), that breaks — fact[n] mod p hits a factor of p and becomes 0, so its inverse doesn't exist. Lucas' theorem rescues this: write n and r in base p as digits (nₖ…n₁n₀) and (rₖ…r₁r₀). Then C(n, r) ≡ ∏ C(nᵢ, rᵢ) (mod p) — the product of the small digit-wise binomials. Each C(nᵢ, rᵢ) has both arguments < p, so the standard factorial+Fermat method (or a tiny table) computes it. If any digit has rᵢ > nᵢ, that factor is 0, so the whole answer is 0.

remember.pattern: Reduce a huge nCr mod a small prime to a product of digit-wise binomials in base p
remember.formula:
write n = (n_k ... n_1 n_0) and r = (r_k ... r_1 r_0) in base p
C(n, r) mod p = product over i of C(n_i, r_i) mod p
if any r_i > n_i: the product (and the answer) is 0
each C(n_i, r_i) with n_i, r_i < p via factorials + Fermat inverse
rules: Use Lucas when **n can exceed p** (p small). The plain factorial method needs `p > n`; Lucas removes that limit.
Process `n` and `r` digit by digit in **base p** (repeatedly take `% p` then `/= p`). The recursion bottoms out when both reach 0.
If at any digit `rᵢ > nᵢ`, then `C(nᵢ, rᵢ) = 0`, which forces the whole product to **0** — short-circuit and return 0.
Each per-digit `C(nᵢ, rᵢ)` has `nᵢ, rᵢ < p`, so precompute factorials and inverse-factorials **up to p−1** once (Fermat inverse) and answer each digit in O(1).

The modulus must be **prime** (Lucas is a statement mod a prime). For prime powers use the generalised Granville/Andrew theorem; combine several primes with CRT. Use **long** in Java for digit products.
whenToUse: Compute `C(n, r) mod p` where `n` is astronomically large (up to 10¹⁸) and `p` is a **small prime**
Counting problems mod a small prime where n far exceeds the modulus
Combined with CRT to get nCr modulo a composite by working over its prime factors
Anywhere the plain factorial-inverse method fails because `p ≤ n`
antiSignals: `p > n` (e.g. p = 1e9+7 and n ≤ 1e6) → the plain factorial + Fermat method is simpler and direct
The modulus is **not prime** → Lucas doesn't apply; use Granville's generalisation or CRT over prime factors
You need an **exact** (non-modular) binomial → big integers / Pascal, no Lucas
n is small enough to build a Pascal triangle mod p → just do that
remember.takeaway: Lucas' theorem says a binomial coefficient modulo a prime is the product of the binomials of the base-p digits. It's the tool for nCr mod p exactly when the factorial method dies — n bigger than p. Precompute factorials and inverses up to p−1 once, peel off base-p digits of n and r together, multiply the per-digit C(nᵢ, rᵢ), and short-circuit to 0 the moment a digit has rᵢ > nᵢ. Pair it with CRT to handle composite moduli.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that the factorial-inverse nCr method requires p > n, why it fails when n ≥ p (fact[n] ≡ 0 mod p has no inverse), and that Lucas' theorem decomposes the coefficient into digit-wise binomials in base p.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Applying the factorial method with n ≥ p (division by a non-invertible factorial), forgetting that rᵢ > nᵢ in any digit makes the whole result 0, or using Lucas with a non-prime modulus.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain WHY n ≥ p breaks the factorial method, state Lucas as C(n,r) ≡ ∏ C(nᵢ,rᵢ) (mod p), note the 0 short-circuit, and mention CRT-over-primes for composite moduli.

problemStatement:
Given integers `n` and `r` and a **prime** `p`, compute the binomial coefficient `C(n, r) mod p`.

The twist versus the standard problem: `n` may be **much larger than `p`** (for example `n` up to `10¹⁸` with `p` a small prime like `13` or `1000003`). The usual 'precompute factorials up to n' approach is impossible (n is too large) and incorrect (factorials contain factors of p). Use Lucas' theorem.
constraints: 0 ≤ r ≤ n ≤ 10¹⁸ (n can vastly exceed p)
p is prime and 2 ≤ p ≤ 10⁶ or so (small enough to precompute factorials up to p−1)
Define C(n, r) = 0 when r > n
Use long in Java for digit products; Python big ints are exact
understanding: When p > n, C(n, r) mod p is just the factorial-inverse formula. But when n ≥ p, that formula is both infeasible (you can't build a length-n factorial table for n = 10¹⁸) and invalid (n! contains factors of p, so n! ≡ 0 mod p and has no inverse). Lucas' theorem provides a different route: it relates C(n, r) mod p to the binomial coefficients of the digits of n and r when both are written in base p. Each digit is below p, so each per-digit binomial is computable with a small factorial table. Multiplying them gives the answer mod p.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is n larger than p?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: That's the whole reason for Lucas. If p > n I'd just use factorials + Fermat. When n ≥ p, those factorials hit a factor of p and the method collapses, so I switch to Lucas.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is p prime?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lucas requires a prime modulus. For a prime power I'd use Granville's generalisation; for a general composite I'd factor it, apply Lucas per prime power, and combine with CRT.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How small is p — can I precompute factorials up to p−1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, p is small (say ≤ 10⁶), so I build fact[0..p−1] and inverse-factorials once with Fermat, then each digit's binomial is O(1).

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if r > n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: C(n, r) = 0. Lucas also returns 0 whenever any base-p digit of r exceeds the corresponding digit of n — I short-circuit there.

examples.explanation: Base 3: 10 = (1 0 1)₃, 3 = (0 1 0)₃. Digit-wise: C(1,0)·C(0,1)·C(1,0). The middle factor C(0,1) = 0 → whole product 0. (Indeed C(10,3)=120, and 120 mod 3 = 0.)
At least one base-13 digit of 500 exceeds the matching digit of 1000, making a factor 0 (C(1000,500) mod 13 = 0).
n, r < p so there's a single digit: C(5,2) = 10, and 10 mod 13 = 10. Lucas reduces to the ordinary binomial here.

approaches.name: Factorial + Fermat Inverse (Baseline — fails when n ≥ p)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first to show you know the standard method AND precisely why it breaks once n ≥ p — that diagnosis motivates Lucas.
hints: The standard nCr mod p uses fact[n]·invFact[r]·invFact[n−r] with Fermat inverses. What two things go wrong when n is 10¹⁸ and p is small?
First, you can't allocate a factorial table of length 10¹⁸. Second — subtler — once n ≥ p, n! is divisible by p, so fact[n] ≡ 0 mod p and has NO inverse.
So the method is both infeasible and mathematically invalid here. You need a formula that works digit-by-digit in base p, keeping every factorial argument below p.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Precomputing fact[0..n] is O(n) time and space, with O(1) per query — but only when p > n. When n ≥ p the table is too large to build and fact[n] is 0 mod p (not invertible), so the approach simply doesn't work.
approaches.explanation:
The textbook method computes `C(n, r) mod p = fact[n]·invFact[r]·invFact[n−r] mod p`, with inverse-factorials from Fermat's little theorem. It is the correct, fast answer **when `p > n`**. The point of this baseline is to see exactly why it fails outside that regime.

**Failure 1 — the table can't exist.** With `n` up to `10¹⁸`, a factorial array of length `n+1` is impossible to allocate. There isn't enough memory in the universe for `10¹⁸` entries.

**Failure 2 — the factorial has no inverse.** Even setting memory aside, the math breaks. Once `n ≥ p`, the product `n! = 1·2·…·n` includes the factor `p` itself, so `n! ≡ 0 (mod p)`. A value of `0` modulo `p` has **no** multiplicative inverse — Fermat's `a^(p−2)` gives `0`, not a true inverse. The formula `fact[n]·invFact[r]·…` would multiply and 'invert' zeros and produce garbage. This is the deep reason the method is restricted to `p > n`, where no factorial argument ever reaches `p`.

**What we actually need.** A method whose every factorial argument stays **below `p`**, so no factor of `p` ever enters and every inverse exists. Lucas' theorem delivers exactly that by working on the base-`p` digits of `n` and `r`, each of which is in `[0, p)`.
approaches.insight: This baseline is the right tool only when p > n. The instant n ≥ p it fails twice over — the table is unbuildable and fact[n] ≡ 0 mod p is non-invertible. Diagnosing those two failures is what tells you to reach for Lucas, which keeps every factorial argument under p.

java.line: return fact[n] * invFact[r] % p * invFact[n - r] % p;
java.explanation: Correct only if p > n; when n ≥ p, fact[n] ≡ 0 mod p so invFact is bogus and this is invalid.

python.explanation: Same restriction: needs p > n; otherwise fact[n] is 0 mod p with no inverse.

pitfalls: Using it when n ≥ p — fact[n] ≡ 0 mod p is not invertible.
Trying to allocate a factorial table for n = 10¹⁸.
Assuming Fermat gives an inverse of 0 — it returns 0, not a real inverse.

approaches.name: Lucas' Theorem (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want when n can exceed a small prime p. Phrase it as 'write n and r in base p; the coefficient is the product of the digit binomials'.

complexity.time: O(p + log_p(n)) — O(p) precompute, O(log_p n) digits per query

hints: Write n and r in base p. Lucas' theorem says C(n, r) ≡ ∏ C(nᵢ, rᵢ) (mod p) over the base-p digits. Each digit is < p — what does that buy you?
Precompute factorials and inverse-factorials only up to p−1 (one Fermat inverse + backward sweep). Then each digit's C(nᵢ, rᵢ) is O(1).
Peel digits with n % p and r % p, multiply the digit binomials, recurse on n / p and r / p. If any rᵢ > nᵢ the digit binomial is 0, so the whole answer is 0 — short-circuit.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Precomputing factorials up to p−1 is O(p) time and space (plus one O(log p) Fermat inverse). A query peels O(log_p n) base-p digits, each costing O(1) via the small tables. So per-query time is O(log_p n) after the O(p) setup.
approaches.explanation:
Lucas' theorem reduces a binomial coefficient modulo a prime to a product of much smaller binomials — the binomials of the base-`p` digits.

**The statement.** Write `n` and `r` in base `p`:

`n = nₖ·pᵏ + … + n₁·p + n₀`,  `r = rₖ·pᵏ + … + r₁·p + r₀`, with each digit in `[0, p)`. Then

`C(n, r) ≡ C(nₖ, rₖ) · … · C(n₁, r₁) · C(n₀, r₀) (mod p)`.

Every factor `C(nᵢ, rᵢ)` has both arguments below `p`, so no factorial argument ever reaches `p` — the inverse problem that killed the baseline never arises.

**Why each digit binomial is cheap.** Since `nᵢ, rᵢ < p`, precompute `fact[0..p−1]` and inverse-factorials up to `p−1` **once** (one Fermat inverse for `fact[p−1]`, then the backward sweep), and `C(nᵢ, rᵢ) = fact[nᵢ]·invFact[rᵢ]·invFact[nᵢ−rᵢ] mod p` is `O(1)`. The setup is `O(p)`, not `O(n)` — that's what makes huge `n` feasible.

**Why a 0 digit zeroes everything.** If for some position `rᵢ > nᵢ`, then `C(nᵢ, rᵢ) = 0` (you can't choose more than you have), and a single zero factor makes the entire product `0 mod p`. So the algorithm can short-circuit and return `0` the moment it sees `rᵢ > nᵢ`. This is why coefficients like `C(10, 3) mod 3` come out `0`: a base-3 digit of `3` exceeds the matching digit of `10`.

**The recursion.** Peel the lowest digits with `nᵢ = n % p`, `rᵢ = r % p`; multiply the running product by `C(nᵢ, rᵢ)`; recurse (or loop) on `n / p`, `r / p`. Stop when `r` becomes `0` — all higher digits of `r` are `0`, and `C(anything, 0) = 1`, so they contribute nothing. There are only `O(log_p n)` digits, so a query is fast even for `n = 10¹⁸`.

**Why p must be prime.** Lucas' theorem is a statement modulo a prime; the proof uses `(1 + x)^p ≡ 1 + x^p (mod p)`, the Freshman's-dream identity that holds only for prime `p`. For a prime power `p^a` there's Granville's generalisation; for a general composite, factor it, apply Lucas modulo each prime (power), and recombine with the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

**Overflow safety.** Digit binomials are products of values below `p`; with `p` up to `~10⁶` the products fit comfortably in a 64-bit `long` as long as you reduce `mod p` after each multiply. Python integers are unbounded, so the modulus is for correctness and speed, not overflow.
approaches.insight: Lucas turns 'huge n, small prime p' into 'a handful of tiny binomials' by reading n and r in base p. The two facts that make it practical: every digit binomial has arguments below p (so a length-p factorial table suffices), and any digit with rᵢ > nᵢ collapses the whole product to 0. It's the natural partner of nCr-mod-p: use factorials+Fermat when p > n, Lucas when p ≤ n, and CRT to glue several primes for composite moduli.

pitfalls: Using Lucas with a non-prime modulus — it only holds mod a prime; use Granville + CRT otherwise.
Forgetting the rᵢ > nᵢ short-circuit — must contribute a 0 factor.
Precomputing factorials up to n instead of p−1 — defeats the purpose for huge n.
Stopping the loop too early — continue while either n or r still has digits.
Letting digit products overflow in Java — reduce mod p after each multiply, use long.

edgeCases.behavior: Single digit: Lucas reduces to the ordinary C(n, r) mod p.
All digits of r are 0, every C(nᵢ, 0) = 1 → result 1.
Some digit has rᵢ > nᵢ (or higher r digits exceed n's) → 0.
Lucas in base 2 gives Kummer's parity: C(n,r) is odd iff r's bits are a subset of n's.

Forgetting that any base-p digit with rᵢ > nᵢ makes the whole result 0.
Using Lucas with a composite modulus instead of a prime.
Precomputing factorials up to n rather than p−1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Factorial method with n ≥ p
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When n ≥ p, n! contains a factor of p, so fact[n] ≡ 0 (mod p) and has no inverse — Fermat returns 0, not a real inverse. The result is meaningless. Use Lucas, which keeps every factorial argument below p.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# n = 10, p = 3:
return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % p * inv_fact[n - r] % p  # fact[10] % 3 == 0
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
lucas = Lucas(p)
return lucas.n_cr(n, r)   # digit-wise binomials, every argument < p

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the zero-digit short-circuit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If any base-p digit of r exceeds the matching digit of n, C(nᵢ, rᵢ) = 0 and the full product must be 0. Skipping that check (e.g. clamping) gives a wrong nonzero answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
long ni = n % p, ri = r % p;
result = result * smallNcr(ni, ri) % p; // smallNcr must return 0 when ri>ni

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Lucas on a composite modulus
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Lucas' theorem holds modulo a prime (its proof uses (1+x)^p ≡ 1+x^p mod p). For a composite m, factor m into prime powers, apply Lucas/Granville per factor, then CRT-combine.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: lucas = Lucas(12)        # 12 is not prime — invalid
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# factor 12 = 4 * 3; compute C(n,r) mod 4 (Granville) and mod 3 (Lucas),
# then combine with CRT to get C(n,r) mod 12

followupVariations.hint: The p > n companion — factorials + Fermat; Lucas reuses the same per-digit binomial.

followupVariations.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
followupVariations.hint: Combine Lucas results modulo several primes to get nCr modulo a composite.

followupVariations.title: Modular Exponentiation

followupVariations.title: Kummer's Theorem
followupVariations.hint: Counts the power of p dividing C(n, r) via base-p carries — the companion to Lucas mod p.

patternNote: Lucas' theorem — nCr modulo a small prime when n exceeds p. Recognise it whenever the factorial method's p > n precondition fails. Decompose into base-p digit binomials, precompute factorials only up to p−1, and short-circuit on a zero digit. Pair with CRT for composite moduli; it's the large-n counterpart of nCr mod p.
